en: The Sūtra on the Conduct of Mañjuśrī,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dhanagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. I,
Dhanagupta, take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana, the Ocean of Great Wisdom.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. All of them were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they possessed the three knowledges and the six superknowledges, were endowed with the eight liberations, and had attained unimpeded wisdom and complete purity. These five hundred bhikṣus each sat cross-legged in their respective rooms, their bodies and minds tranquil as they entered right samādhi.

At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, desiring to inspire his own practice of the Dharma and to cause the assembly to hear and know it so as to obtain great benefit, rose first of all and proceeded one by one to survey all the cells. He then saw the Venerable Śāriputra dwelling alone in a cell, having subdued his body, sitting cross-legged, and entered into samādhi.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, having seen this, did not awaken [the others], but went to various places to inspect the other rooms, proceeding in this manner until the morning when the sun first rose.

At that time, Śāriputra and the five hundred bhikṣus had all emerged from meditative concentration; these bhikṣus, along with other bhikṣus who had come from various directions, and the entire great assembly, had all gathered like clouds.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat; with body upright and composed, he proceeded with slow and deliberate steps, walking with the steady gait of a lion king, and went out from his own chamber to the prepared seat.
The entire assembly surrounded him on all sides; out of reverent mindfulness of the World-Honored One, they did not dare to stand before him.

At that time, the World-Honored One stood as the supreme leader amidst the great multitude; his radiant countenance was majestic like a mountain of gold, and he rode upon the clouds of great compassion to rain down the showers of the Dharma.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Venerable Śāriputra in the midst of the great assembly, saying:
"Just now, as I surveyed all the rooms, I saw you alone in one room, sitting cross-legged with your body held erect. Were you at that time practicing dhyāna, or not?"
The Venerable Śāriputra replied to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying,
"At that time, I was indeed practicing dhyāna.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked Śāriputra again:
"What do you think? Do you wish to practice sitting meditation in order to eliminate that which has not yet been severed?
Or do you wish to practice sitting meditation in order to further sever and eliminate that which has already been severed?"
Is one practicing meditation by relying on the phenomena of the three periods of time—past, present, and future?
Or is one practicing meditation by relying on the phenomena of the five aggregates—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Is one practicing seated meditation by relying on the various faculties— the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—
or is one practicing seated meditation by relying on the six objects— forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena?
Is one practicing dhyāna by relying on the three realms of existence—namely, the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm?
Or is one practicing dhyāna by relying on the internal, the external, or the distinction between the internal and external phenomena?
"Do you practice meditation by relying on the body, or the mind, or both body and mind—that is, on the phenomena of name-and-form?
I have asked you about such matters; you should answer quickly: upon what do you rely when practicing meditation?"
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra replied to Mañjuśrī, saying: "Virtuous one!
I now personally perceive the joyful practice of all dharmas; it is because of mindfulness and non-forgetfulness that I sit in dhyāna."
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī further questioned Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra,
are there truly any dharmas that can be perceived through direct vision, which a practitioner of joy might remember without forgetting?”
Śāriputra said: "O worthy Mañjuśrī!
As for such a dharma of joyful practice, I truly do not perceive it."
"O virtuous Mañjuśrī!

Although I do not personally see such a dharma of joyful practice, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has indeed taught the dharma of tranquil concentration to all the assemblies of śrāvakas; it is according to such a dharma that I practice."
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"What dharmas did the Tathāgata formerly teach to the assembly of śrāvakas as 'peaceful concentration,' which you rely upon for practice?"
Śāriputra said: "Venerable Mañjuśrī!
There is a bhikṣu who practices in reliance upon all dharmas of the past, future, and present; briefly stated, he even practices in reliance upon all dharmas such as mind and intellect."
"Just as those who practice the Dharma, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught this tranquility for the sake of all the assembly of śrāvakas; I practice in accordance with it.
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva again asked the Venerable Śāriputra:

"As for your statement, 'The Tathāgata once taught that for the sake of all the assembly of śrāvakas, [he spoke of] those three times, up to mind and mental faculty, and I practice in accordance with it'—this is not so."

Why is this? Because that Tathāgata of the past does not exist in the present; that Tathāgata of the future does not exist in the present; and that Tathāgata of the present does not exist [as such] in the past.
If this is so, then when one seeks the body of the Tathāgata within all dharmas, it is entirely unattainable.
Why do you now speak these words: "I act in reliance upon the dharmas of the past, future, and present"?

O Śāriputra! Regarding the past limit, as well as the future and present limits, that does not become this, nor does this become that; each is distinct and separate, not acting for the sake of the other. They have no location, nor do they have a basis for abiding, nor is there anyone who abides; no place of reliance can be found.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if anyone should say that the past, future, and present exist within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), whether asserting they have a basis or asserting they are without a basis, you should know that such persons slander the Tathāgata and incur a grave and heavy offense.
Why is this so? That true reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is without recollection and without thought, nor does it fall away;
it possesses no form or color, and no characteristic mark can be apprehended therein.

O Śāriputra! Within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the dharmas of the past, future, and present are truly unobtainable; briefly stated, even dharmas such as mind (*citta*) and intellect (*manas*) are unobtainable.
Apart from the limit of reality, not a single dharma can be found.
"For this reason, it is said that they are called 'empty'; because they are empty, there are no phenomena, and thus nothing can be manifested or explained.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Can the Tathāgata not abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) while teaching the Dharma?"
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī replied to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra,
within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), what location exists such that the Tathāgata would dwell in the reality-limit to teach all dharmas?"
Śāriputra! Since phenomena are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, how could the Tathāgata, having abided in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), speak of all phenomena?
Not only are phenomena non-existent, but the Tathāgata is also non-existent.
Since they do not exist, how can it be said that the Tathāgata, having abided in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), has taught all dharmas? Why is this so?
Because all dharmas are ultimately unattainable.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he is truly unattainable.
The essence of the Dharma he teaches is also thus: it is unattainable in time, unattainable outside of time, and unattainable both in time and outside of time.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as manifesting either during the time of speaking or during the time of not speaking.
Why is this so? Śāriputra, the Tathāgata has severed all paths of speech; he is unconditioned, uncreated, and without any fixed location.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
According to what you have said, who here is capable of being a vessel for the Dharma?"
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī then replied to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra!
If there is anyone who can dismantle conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and yet does not enter into nirvāṇa, such a person is capable of being a vessel for the Dharma."

Furthermore, if one can neither realize nor speak of past phenomena, neither realize nor speak of future phenomena, and neither realize nor speak of present phenomena, such a person is capable of being a vessel for the Dharma.
One who has neither views of affliction nor views of purification, and no view of the conditioned or the unconditioned, is a fit vessel for this teaching.
One for whom there is neither self nor non-self, and who neither grasps nor rejects within the sphere of activity, is a fit vessel for this teaching.
"Such a person, although able to hear and receive [the teaching], does not take what has been spoken therein as a definitive, literal exposition.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again asked the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"If it is as you have said, how should one practice regarding this meaning?"
"How does one abide according to the teaching?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva then addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!..."
If this meaning were such that words could be employed, one might ask, "How does the teaching abide?
Since within this meaning there are no words and all mental activities have been severed, how can you ask, "How does the teaching abide?"
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “O worthy Mañjuśrī!
This meaning is exceedingly profound; within this meaning, there are few who have realized it through direct knowledge, and few who uphold it.”

Why is this? For even all those in training and the Arhats are still lost and submerged within this stage; how much more so for ordinary worldlings—how could they possibly know or comprehend such a profound meaning?
Mañjuśrī said, “Śāriputra!
Among these meanings, the arhats have no ground; therefore, there is no ground upon which the arhats can abide.”
Because of non-abiding, one is called an Arhat; because of non-attainment, one is called an Arhat; because the path of speech is cut off, one is called an Arhat.
Because the path of speech is cut off, there is no place of realization for those who practice within the stages of an Arhat.

Because there is no place of realization, those who practice on the level of an Arhat are designated by the name "unconditioned dharma" (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); because they do not arise, they are called unconditioned. There is no agent, nor is there any place of abiding.
What is called the stage of attainment for an arhat?
Those who are arhats are not called "arhats" by virtue of name,
nor are they called "arhats" by virtue of form.
Only ordinary worldlings falsely engage in conceptual discrimination within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); yet such name-and-form is actually devoid of discrimination.
All Arhats likewise understand this and do not give rise to discrimination; therefore, Arhats are called "Arhats" because they do not rely on name nor on form.
There is no ordinary person, nor are there any dharmas of an ordinary person; there is no arhat, nor are there any dharmas of an arhat that can be apprehended.
Therefore, the arhat does not engage in conceptual discrimination. Because he practices non-action, there is no sphere of activity, no agent, and this is itself tranquil concentration.
One does not act as one who exists, nor as one who does not exist, nor as one who neither exists nor does not exist.

Since non-action and the unconditioned cannot be apprehended therein, one attains detachment from all existence; with no mind and no formations to be apprehended, it is said that one is definitively and correctly established within the fruits of the śramaṇa.
At that time, while the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was speaking thus, five hundred bhikṣus rose from their seats in the great assembly and cried out in a loud voice before the World-Honored One:

"From this day forward, we shall no longer wish to see the body of Mañjuśrī, nor shall we wish to hear his name. We should quickly abandon such places and locations; we shall never again approach any dwelling place where Mañjuśrī resides."
"Why is this? How does Mañjuśrī speak of the single characteristic of affliction and liberation?
Having simultaneously raised their voices to utter these words, the five hundred bhikṣus all turned their backs on the assembly and departed.
They further thought:

"How is it that after we have joyfully delighted in learning and practiced the holy life within the Dharma taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One himself, we have suddenly heard such a base and evil teaching today?"
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
"Do you not wish for all sentient beings to decisively understand such a Dharma as you have described?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied, "It is so, it is so."
The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Mañjuśrī!

If it is as you say, why is it that these five hundred bhikṣus have risen from their seats to revile and slander what you have spoken? Why do they stand before the Buddha, crying out in a loud voice: 'There is no need to see Mañjuśrī, nor is there any need to hear the name of Mañjuśrī; this region must also be abandoned, and one must never go to any dwelling place where Mañjuśrī resides'? Having uttered these words, they left the assembly.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta praised the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You, Śāriputra, have skillfully and well spoken those words of proclamation uttered by those bhikṣus."
Why is this? Because in reality, Mañjuśrī cannot be apprehended.
If, in reality, Mañjuśrī cannot be apprehended, then he likewise cannot be seen and cannot be heard; thus, that direction must also be relinquished.
Why is this so? Because all the dwelling places of Mañjuśrī, as well as those places and Mañjuśrī himself, are non-existent;
that which is non-existent cannot even be approached, and must be relinquished.
At that time, while the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was speaking thus, five hundred bhikṣus returned to the assembly and addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"What you have spoken, O Noble One, was not for us; how could we possibly understand what you have said?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī praised the bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! It is so, it is so!
Regarding this Dharma, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of śrāvakas should act in this manner; they need not seek to know it."
In this Dharma, the bhikṣus must also act in this way; it is not that they need not know it, nor is it that they do not need to know it. Why is this so?
Such a dharma is eternally abiding and is also called the *dharmadhātu*.

That which is eternally abiding and the *dharmadhātu* is without recollection and without mindfulness. Being without recollection and without mindfulness, there is nothing that is realized and nothing that is not realized. Since there is nothing that is not realized, it is also neither non-realization, nor non-recollection, nor non-mindfulness.
"If one knows in this way, they are called a true śrāvaka disciple of the Tathāgata; they are named 'supreme' and may be said to be 'worthy of offerings' (arhat).

At that time, while the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was speaking these words, among that assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, four hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of mind through the outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). One hundred bhikṣus, however, increased their disparagement and gave rise to a mind of slander; in their very present bodies, they fell headlong into the great hells.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
Why do you not preach the Dharma in accordance with sentient beings?"
"This will cause one hundred bhikṣus to fall away and lose their attainments.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"You, Śāriputra, should not speak such words."
Why is this? Śāriputra,
if these one hundred bhikṣus had not heard this profound root of the Dharma, you should know that they would certainly have fallen into the great hells and suffered there for an entire kalpa.
After emerging from hell, they will finally obtain a human body and a human rebirth.

Because those bhikṣus have heard this profound meaning of the Dharma-fundament, all their evil karma and heavy offenses—which would otherwise have caused them to fall into the great Avīci hell to suffer for an eon—have, today, been experienced in a single instant upon entering the Mahāraurava hell; immediately thereafter, they attain rebirth in the Tuṣita heaven to enjoy the various celestial pleasures.
"Śāriputra, you should know that because these bhikṣus have heard this Dharma, they will swiftly eliminate their many sins and undergo only a brief, slight retribution.

Śāriputra, you should know that these one hundred bhikṣus, at the first assembly when Maitreya Bodhisattva descends to be born and attains enlightenment, shall attain the fruit of Arhatship among the śrāvaka assembly. They will exhaust all outflows (āsrava), be free from further afflictions, and possess the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā), the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa); both the remaining traces of mental and physical afflictions will be completely exhausted."

Therefore, Śāriputra, it would be better to listen to and receive this Dharma with a mind of doubt than to achieve the state of mind of the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables, nor even to fully achieve the state of mind of the four formless absorptions.

Why is this? Although one may have accomplished such dharmas, if they do not hear this profound root of the Dharma, they will not attain liberation from afflictions, nor from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Out of compassion for these people, I shall speak this fundamental teaching.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “How rare! How rare!”
“Mañjuśrī is indeed able to skillfully expound such a fundamental teaching of the Dharma for the sake of transforming and guiding all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: “Śāriputra!
The limit of reality neither increases nor decreases; the dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases; and the realm of sentient beings likewise has no increase or decrease. Why is this so?

Regarding such dharmas as these, they exist only as verbal designations and nothing can be apprehended therein; that does not produce this, and this does not produce that. Since there is no self-nature in the self, what basis for dependence could there be?
Therefore, Śāriputra, awakening (bodhi) is itself liberation. Why is this?
Because all dharmas and wisdom have no distinct location; they are neither produced nor unproduced.
"If one knows in this way, they are said to have already entered nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!"
It is so, it is so, just as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has said.

Within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is neither increase nor decrease; likewise, within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), there is neither increase nor decrease, for they do not undergo affliction nor do they undergo liberation.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words, in order to further clarify the meaning of ultimate reality, he spoke again in sublime verses:
"Phenomena of the past, present, and future Are mere words and lack true reality;
If they were in the state of reality, They would be of a single characteristic, without distinction."
If there is no conceptualization of signs, this is precisely the reality of signs;
when there are no signs and no conceptualization, conceptualization itself is signless.
If one does not engage in conceptualization, one will not discern nirvana.
Both of these are the works of Māra; the wise should recognize them.
Within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, although I have spoken of them by name, that which is nameless and unarisen—those two are, in turn, of one single characteristic.
When the mind arises with correct discrimination, it immediately becomes a false thought;
for sublime wisdom is non-conceptual, because it possesses the practice of emptiness.
Discrimination involves deliberation, whereas non-discrimination is without thought.
Discrimination is itself a sign; by not discriminating, one attains nirvāṇa.
If one can know in this way, they are called one of great wisdom.
Therefore, the knower of exhaustion attains a wisdom free from conceptual differentiation.
Wisdom can speak of wisdom, yet the speaking of wisdom is itself empty;
one who can endure this within it is called one of great wisdom.
Even if one were to fill the three thousandfold world-system with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, [it would not equal the merit of such endurance].
For one who endures and has faith in this Dharma, their merit shall be supreme.
Even if, throughout billions of eons, one were to achieve the merit of giving,
precepts, patience, diligence, supernatural powers, and eloquence, it would not equal that of upholding this sutra.
"If those who uphold this sutra, the Tathāgatas shall declare that by the power of the merit of this sutra, they shall all attain Buddhahood. At that time,
when the World-Honored One spoke these verses from the *Dharmapada-sūtra*, ten thousand beings of various kinds became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Five hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of mind within the outflow-free dharmas;
eighty thousand devaputras of the desire realm who had not yet resolved their minds all gave rise to the thought of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed upon them this prediction:
"In the Constellation Kalpa, you shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; you shall all share the same title, namely, Dharma-ārambha-puṣpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the youth Mañjuśrī, the Venerable Śāriputra, and the five hundred bhikṣus, along with the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, and so forth—and all the spirits and ghosts, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Mañjuśrīśrī (The Scripture of Mañjuśrī)
